title: What qualifications does a trainer or assessor need to work for an RTO in Australia?
description: Credential Policy rules for RTO trainers and assessors: TAE40122, assessor skill sets, working under direction, industry experts, TAE delivery and CPD.
shortAnswer: Under the 2025 Standards for RTOs and the Credential Policy, a trainer who makes assessment judgments without direction needs TAE40122, TAE40116 or TAE40110 Certificate IV in Training and Assessment, a diploma or higher in adult education or VET, or a secondary teaching qualification with a listed skill set. Others may train only under the direction of a credentialled trainer. Every trainer also needs current industry competencies at least to the level being taught.
keyTakeaways: Standard 3.2 of the Outcome Standards requires training and assessment to be delivered only by people holding the credentials in the Credential Policy, plus continuing professional development in training and assessment.
Standard 3.3 separately requires industry competencies at least to the level of the training product and an understanding of current industry practice. A TAE qualification alone is not enough.
People enrolled in TAE40122 or TAE50122 can train under direction only while making progress to finish within two years of commencement, and cannot make assessment judgments.
Industry experts engaged under Standard 3.3 must work under the direction of a credentialled trainer and assess alongside a trainer or assessor, never alone.
The current Credential Policy is the version of December 10, 2025, which corrected formatting only. The content is unchanged from the policy that commenced on July 1, 2025.
regulator: Australian Skills Quality Authority (ASQA), applying the National Vocational Education and Training Regulator (Outcome Standards for Registered Training Organisations) Instrument 2025 and the Credential Policy published by the Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
appliesTo: Trainers, assessors and validators working for or on behalf of ASQA regulated RTOs
Enterprise RTOs that use their own subject matter experts as trainers
Industry experts brought in to deliver specialist training
Employers who buy accredited training and audit their provider's trainer files

sections.heading: Which rules set trainer and assessor credentials?

blocks.text: Two documents work together. Part 3 of the [Outcome Standards instrument](https://www.legislation.gov.au/F2025L00354/asmade/text), Quality Area 3 (VET workforce), sets the outcomes: Standard 3.1 on workforce management, Standard 3.2 on trainer and assessor credentials, and Standard 3.3 on industry skills. The [Credential Policy](https://content.training.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-12/Credential%20Policy%2010%20December%202025.pdf) lists the qualifications that count for each role and states that it "cannot be read as a standalone document".

This page focuses on how an RTO staffs and documents those roles. The wider 2025 Standards, including assessment, validation and recognition of prior learning, are covered in [the 2025 Standards for RTOs](/regulations/standards-for-rtos-2025-training-and-assessment). The Outcome Standards instrument applies to RTOs regulated by ASQA; RTOs regulated only by the Victorian or Western Australian state regulators should confirm their own requirements.

blocks.title: Currency
blocks.text: As at November 2026, ASQA links to the Credential Policy dated December 10, 2025. Its version history records only formatting corrections to Sections 1A and 1B, with no content changes. The Outcome Standards instrument F2025L00354 has had no compilations since it was registered on March 14, 2025.

sections.heading: What can each credential level do?

blocks.text: The Credential Policy creates a ladder of roles. The key line is the assessment judgment: only Section 1A and 1B credential holders can make one, and only Section 1A and 1E credential holders can supervise others.

blocks.text: Two conditions on Section 1D are easy to miss. The RTO must ensure the credential "is relevant to their role, taking into account the nature of the VET student cohort and the delivery context", and must be able to justify that relevance. A volunteer trainer skill set may suit one cohort and not another.

sections.heading: What does working under direction require?

blocks.text: Direction is an active quality assurance role, not a sign off. Section 1E says the person giving direction is "responsible for providing oversight, guidance and quality assurance" for someone without the full credential. Standard 3.2(2)(b) requires the RTO to have systems ensuring that people under direction do not make assessment judgments and are delivering quality training and assessment.

In practice an auditor will look for a named directing trainer for each person under direction, evidence of what that oversight involved, and assessment records showing the judgment was made and signed by a 1A or 1B credential holder. For Section 1C trainees, the RTO should also hold enrollment evidence and progress records, because the two year completion window is a condition of the role.

sections.heading: What industry skills and experts rules apply under Standard 3.3?

blocks.text: Standard 3.3 requires everyone delivering training or assessment, for or on behalf of the RTO, to have industry competencies, skills and knowledge relevant to, and at least to the level of, the training product, and to maintain an understanding of current industry practice. This applies to 1A credential holders as much as to anyone else.

items: An RTO may engage experts by reference to the training product or the specific student cohort, and in response to a specific need.
Experts must have industry competencies and specialized subject matter expertise directly relevant to the product they deliver.
Experts may only work under the direction of a person holding a Section 1E credential.
Where an expert is involved in an assessment judgment, they "conduct the assessment alongside the trainer or assessor".
The training or assessment an expert delivers must be subject to oversight by the RTO.

blocks.text: This is the pathway for enterprise RTOs that want senior technical staff to teach. A plant engineer without a TAE credential can deliver a specialist session, but the RTO must document the need, the direction arrangement and the joint assessment. See [unit of competency](/glossary/unit-of-competency) for the level the industry competency must match.

sections.heading: What extra credentials apply to delivering TAE qualifications?

blocks.text: Section 2 sets a higher bar for the Training and Education (TAE) Training Package itself. To deliver any TAE qualification or skill set, the trainer must hold it at least to the level being delivered. To deliver TAE40122 or the TAESS00019 Assessor Skill Set, the trainer needs a Diploma of Vocational Education and Training (TAE50122, TAE50116 or TAE50111), a Diploma of Training Design and Development (TAE50216 or TAE50211), or a higher level qualification in adult education or VET.

Certificate IV holders can deliver TAE40122, TAESS00019 or TAESS00024 only under the direction of a diploma level trainer (Sections 2B and 2C). For validation of TAE products that permit assessment judgments, Section 3B requires at least one validator with a qualification or skill set at least to the level being validated.

sections.heading: How are diploma, secondary teaching and CPD requirements defined?

blocks.text: The Credential Policy glossary defines a diploma or higher level qualification in adult education or VET as one at Australian Qualifications Framework level 5 or higher focused on training and assessing adults. It need not have those words in its title, but the academic transcript must show units demonstrating the skills to train adults and teach VET. A secondary teaching qualification is one from a higher education provider that would meet the academic requirements for secondary teacher registration in at least one state or territory. See [AQF levels](/regulations/aqf-levels-and-learning-outcomes).

On professional development, Standard 3.1 requires the RTO to facilitate access to continuing professional development for staff, and Standard 3.2(2)(c) requires it to show how all trainers and assessors undertake CPD to maintain current skills and knowledge in training and assessment, "including skills and knowledge relating to engaging and supporting VET students". Industry currency under Standard 3.3 is a separate obligation, so most RTOs keep two CPD streams per trainer.

sections.heading: How does Knowledge Foundry approach this?

blocks.text: Knowledge Foundry links each trainer to the units they deliver through the same framework that defines those units, so a trainer's credential section and industry competency can be checked against the exact product level before a cohort starts. See how this supports [higher education and VET providers](/industries/higher-education).

faqs.q: Is the Workplace Trainer Skill Set enough to assess students?
faqs.a: No. TAESS00020 Workplace Trainer Skill Set is a Section 1D credential. Its holder can deliver training and contribute to assessment, including collecting evidence, but only under direction and without making assessment judgments. Judgments require a Section 1A or 1B credential.

faqs.q: Can a qualified school teacher train for an RTO without a TAE qualification?
faqs.a: A secondary teaching qualification on its own allows training and assessment under direction only, under Section 1D. Adding TAESS00011, TAESS00019 or TAESS00024 brings the person into Section 1A, allowing training and assessment without direction.

faqs.q: Do holders of the older TAE40110 still qualify?
faqs.a: Yes. TAE40110 Certificate IV in Training and Assessment is listed in Sections 1A, 1B, 1E and 3A of the Credential Policy, alongside TAE40116 and TAE40122. Holders still need industry competency and CPD under Standards 3.2 and 3.3.

faqs.q: What happens if a trainer enrolled in TAE40122 stops progressing?
faqs.a: Section 1C only applies while the person is making satisfactory progress to complete within two years of commencement. If that stops, they no longer qualify under 1C and would need another credential, such as a Section 1D skill set, to keep delivering under direction.

factCheck.claim: Standard 3.2: training and assessment only delivered by persons holding credentials in the Credential Policy; systems so persons under direction do not make assessment judgements; CPD in training and assessment including engaging and supporting VET students

Standard 3.3: industry competencies at least to the level of the training product; current industry practice; experts engaged for specific need, under direction of a credentialled person, assess alongside the trainer, subject to oversight. Standard 3.1 facilitates access to CPD

Credential Policy Sections 1A to 1E list credentials for training and assessment, assessment only, actively working towards (TAE40122 or TAE50122, complete within two years), under direction (skill sets incl TAESS00020, TAESS00015, secondary teaching), and providing direction
Section 1D: RTO must ensure credential is relevant to the role considering the cohort and delivery context and be able to justify relevance
Section 2A: delivering TAE40122 or TAESS00019 requires TAE50122/TAE50116/TAE50111, TAE50216/TAE50211 or higher; Section 2B/2C direction by diploma holder; Section 3B validation of TAE products

Glossary: diploma or higher-level qualification means AQF level 5 or higher focused on training adults, title need not include the words, transcript evidence; secondary teaching qualification defined by registration requirements in at least one State or Territory
